```{r a4-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

Grading geographic areas on multiple socioeconomic outcomes requires a common
ordering rule even when two outcomes rank areas differently or differ in
precision. Here we grade all `67` Alabama counties across adult household
income rank and adult incarceration rate using `pr_case_alabama`, then compare
that shared grading against separate single-outcome gradings.

Higher priority (grade 1) corresponds to more favorable historical cohort
outcomes: higher adult income and lower incarceration (rather than greater
funding need). Sharing a grade leaves two counties unordered without claiming
equal outcomes. All posterior inputs and optimization results below are stored
in the package and loaded without fitting a model or running a solver during
rendering.

## Cohort, outcome dates, and source license {#whose-outcomes-are-being-compared}

```{r a4-load}
library(postrank)
alabama <- pr_case_alabama
```

`pr_case_alabama` is adapted from Chetty, Friedman, Hendren, Jones, and Porter
(2022), *Replication Data for: The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood
Roots of Social Mobility* (Harvard Dataverse V1.0,
[doi:10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1); source:
Opportunity Insights and the U.S. Census Bureau), distributed under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) (no endorsement by
the original authors or agencies is implied; see `?pr_case_alabama` and the
installed `DATA-NOTICE.md`).

The observations describe children born in `1978-1983` whose parents were at
the 25th national income percentile, pooled across race and gender, across all
`67` Alabama counties (2010 Census county boundaries; every county has both
published estimates and positive standard errors):

- **Adult income (`income`)**: mean household income percentile rank (`0` to
  `100` percentile points), measured from `2014-2015` tax records.
- **Incarceration (`incarceration`)**: percentage residing in a correctional
  facility on `April 1, 2010` (a single-day Census snapshot rather than
  lifetime incarceration or current crime; see the
  [Opportunity Atlas codebook](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Codebook-for-Table-2.pdf)).

These historical conditional outcomes do not identify the causal effect of
growing up in a county or of changing local policy today. Below are four
example counties from `alabama$units` before posterior shrinkage:

```{r a4-observations}
show <- match(c("Baldwin County", "Coosa County", "Crenshaw County",
  "Russell County"), alabama$units$county_name)
observed <- alabama$units[show, c("county_name", "income_estimate_points",
  "income_se_points", "incarceration_estimate_points",
  "incarceration_se_points")]
knitr::kable(observed, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
  col.names = c("County", "Income rank", "Income SE",
    "Incarceration (%)", "Incarceration SE"))
```

Published standard errors already combine sampling error and Census privacy
noise, so they enter the observation model once without adding a second
privacy variance; the published cohort-count column is descriptive rather than
a binomial denominator or loss weight.

## Separate posterior models and target orientation

Each outcome was fitted separately across the `67` Alabama counties using a
Gaussian observation likelihood around a logistic-normal county random effect.
The logit-scale intercept had a normal prior with standard deviation `1.5` and
mean `qlogis(0.40)` for income or `qlogis(0.03)` for incarceration. The
between-county logit standard deviation had a half-normal prior with scale
`1`. To align priority directions so larger values mean more favorable
outcomes on both criteria, `income` is `100` times the latent income rank
fraction (percentile points) and `incarceration` is `-100` times the latent
incarceration probability (negative percentage points, so `-1` ranks above
`-4`).

`alabama$input` is a `postrank_probabilities` object built from MCMC pool A
(the primary `16,000`-draw MCMC run per criterion in the source study, compared
with a second `8,000`-draw MCMC run, pool B, in the final section), storing the
`67 x 67 x 2` directional-error probabilities together with 95% equal-tail
marginal intervals (`level = 0.95`). Fitting the two criteria separately
preserves within-criterion cross-county dependence and suffices for the
additive weighted loss below, while leaving joint simultaneous-improvement
probabilities and raw MCMC chains unavailable:

```{r a4-means}
posterior_means <- postrank_posterior_means(alabama$input)
data.frame(
  County = alabama$units$county_name[show],
  round(posterior_means[show, ], 2),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

## Two-criterion loss, grades, and criterion error rates {#choose-the-question-for-the-common-report}

In this example, we weight directional errors on `income` and `incarceration`
equally (`0.5` and `0.5`), set the unordered-pair cost to `tau = 0.20`, and
allow up to `G_max = 5` grades:

```{r a4-settings}
settings <- postrank_settings(
  weights = c(income = 0.5, incarceration = 0.5),
  tau = 0.20, G_max = 5L
)
```

Equal weights average the directional-error probabilities across the two
criteria rather than adding income percentile points to incarceration percentage
points.
Recomputing the grading requires a solver (Gurobi is the default and needs a
license; `backend = "highs"` uses `highs` from `install.packages("highs")`).
The solver call is shown below with `eval = FALSE`, and the stored result from
an equivalent call is loaded with `postrank_example()`:

```{r a4-optional-fresh-fit, eval=FALSE}
common <- postrank(
  alabama$input, settings = settings, level = 0.95,
  backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 30, threads = 1L, seed = 1304L),
  fragility = FALSE
)
```

```{r a4-result}
common <- postrank_example("case_alabama67")
common
```

The common grading uses all `5` permitted grades (`1 / 31 / 32 / 1 / 2`
counties), ordering `1,249` of the `2,211` county pairs (`56.5%`) and leaving
`962` pairs unordered, with loss `0.150394` compared with `0.200000` for
leaving all pairs unordered:

```{r a4-grade-sizes}
grades <- get_grades(common)
grade_sizes <- as.data.frame(table(grades), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(grade_sizes) <- c("Grade", "Counties")
knitr::kable(grade_sizes, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r a4-profile}
profile <- get_profile(common)
knitr::kable(profile[, c("criterion", "E", "E_over_N", "risk")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Criterion", "Expected wrong directions",
    "Errors per ordered pair", "Criterion loss"))
```

Across the `1,249` ordered pairs, expected wrong-direction errors per ordered
pair are `5.2%` (`0.0520`) on `income` and `17.2%` (`0.1724`) on
`incarceration`. The solver finished with status `"optimal"` and optimization
gap `1.11e-16`, which measures agreement between the checked grading and the
solver's lower bound on the pool-A probability array rather than Monte Carlo
or model uncertainty.

## Report card for selected counties {#read-counties-within-the-common-grades}

To keep county labels readable, `max_rows = 12` displays `12` counties spanning
all `5` grades (all `67` counties enter the optimization and remain in
`as.data.frame(common)`; pass `max_rows = NULL` on a tall canvas to plot every
county):

```{r a4-report-card, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Posterior means and 95% equal-tail marginal intervals on adult income rank and negated incarceration rate for 12 selected Alabama counties across grades 1 to 5.", fig.alt="Two-panel horizontal dot-and-interval report card for 12 Alabama counties across grades 1 through 5 on income rank (percentile points) and lower incarceration (negative percentage points)."}
units_df <- alabama$units
county_names <- setNames(units_df[["county_name"]], units_df[["entity_id"]])
postrank_plot_report_card(common, max_rows = 12,
  entity_labels = county_names,
  criterion_labels = c(
    income = "Income rank\n(percentile points)",
    incarceration = "Lower incarceration\n(negative percentage points)"
  )
)
```

`Crenshaw County` (`"01041"`) is the sole county in grade `1`, with posterior
mean adult income rank `40.4` percentile points and posterior mean
incarceration rate `0.67%` (`-0.67` on the negated scale). `Montgomery County`
(`"01101"`) and `Russell County` (`"01113"`) share grade `5`, so their mutual
comparison is left unordered. Horizontal bars show 95% marginal intervals for
each county's target one county at a time rather than simultaneous bands or
intervals for the integer grades.

To build a full 67-county membership table with names and Census FIPS codes:

```{r a4-membership}
membership <- data.frame(
  county_id = names(grades),
  county = unname(county_names[names(grades)]),
  grade = unname(grades)
)
head(membership[order(membership$grade, membership$county), ], 8)
```

## Comparing expected-rank cuts and single-outcome gradings {#what-changes-when-each-outcome-gets-its-own-report}

`alabama$reference$actions` stores single-criterion gradings optimized for
income alone (`D1`) and incarceration alone (`D2`), an all-unordered vector
(`B0`), and an expected-rank contiguous-cut rule (`B3`, which sorts counties by
weighted expected rank and chooses optimal contiguous cutpoints along that
fixed order). Below we evaluate all four fixed vectors on the two-criterion
loss using `postrank_compare()`:

```{r a4-compare}
comparison <- postrank_compare(common,
  `Expected-rank cuts` = alabama$reference$actions$B3,
  `Income alone` = alabama$reference$actions$D1,
  `Incarceration alone` = alabama$reference$actions$D2,
  `Withhold all` = alabama$reference$actions$B0,
  baselines = character()
)
knitr::kable(comparison$table[, c("method", "risk", "N", "G")],
  digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Report", "Two-criterion loss", "Ordered pairs", "Grades"))
```

```{r a4-comparison-plot, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Two-criterion loss (weights 0.5/0.5, tau = 0.20, G_max = 5) on pool A for the common grading and four fixed reference gradings.", fig.alt="Comparison plot showing identical two-criterion loss of 0.150394 for joint and Expected-rank cuts, 0.190573 for Income alone, 0.199764 for Incarceration alone, and 0.200000 for Withhold all."}
postrank_plot_compare(comparison)
```

In this dataset, the unrestricted common grading (`joint`) and the
expected-rank cut rule (`B3`) produce identical grades and pair relations
(loss `0.150394`, `1,249` ordered pairs), so joint mixed-integer programming
(MIP) search offers zero loss reduction beyond `B3` here (while additionally
supplying an unrestricted lower bound across all 5-grade groupings). Evaluating
`D1` (`Income alone`) and `D2` (`Incarceration alone`) on the two-criterion
loss gives `0.190573` and `0.199764`.

Conversely, we can evaluate how much extra single-criterion loss the shared
common grading incurs on each outcome relative to `D1` and `D2` on their own
objectives:

```{r a4-single-criterion}
single <- alabama$reference$single_criterion
single_loss <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(single)), function(i) {
  crit <- single$criterion[i]
  postrank_evaluate(alabama$reference$actions[[single$method[i]]],
    alabama$alternatives[[crit]], weights = setNames(1, crit),
    tau = 0.20)$primary_risk
}, numeric(1))
common_loss <- profile$risk[match(single$criterion, profile$criterion)]
cost <- data.frame(
  Criterion = single$criterion,
  Common = common_loss,
  Separate = single_loss,
  Difference = common_loss - single_loss,
  Archived_gap = single$gap
)
knitr::kable(cost, digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Criterion", "Common loss", "Separate loss",
    "Extra loss for common grades", "Separate solver gap"))
```

Requiring one shared grading across both outcomes adds `0.054824` expected loss
on `income` (`0.116403` versus `0.061578`) and `0.064528` on `incarceration`
(`0.184385` versus `0.119857`), for an equal-weight average extra loss of
`0.059676` (measured in expected-loss units rather than dollars or posterior
score intervals).

## Numerical replication across MCMC pools A and B {#check-numerical-repetition-without-changing-the-observations}

`alabama$alternatives$pool_B` comes from a second MCMC run (`8,000` retained
draws per criterion versus `16,000` in pool A) fitted to the exact same 67
county estimates and priors. Comparing pool A and pool B checks Monte Carlo
integration stability without adding new data:

```{r a4-pool-check}
ev_A <- postrank_evaluate(grades, alabama$input, settings = settings)
ev_B <- postrank_evaluate(grades, alabama$alternatives$pool_B,
  settings = settings)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Pool = c("A (16,000 draws)", "B (8,000 draws)"),
  Fixed_report_loss = c(ev_A$primary_risk, ev_B$primary_risk),
  Ordered_pairs = c(ev_A$N, ev_B$N)
), digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

Evaluating the pool-A grading on pool B shifts the loss by `-0.000051`
(`0.150394` to `0.150342`), and re-optimizing on pool B in the source study
changed `0` of the `2,211` pair relations
(`alabama$reference$relation_stability`). In the source chain diagnostics
(`alabama$reference$numerical_pools`), pool B's pairwise Monte Carlo standard
errors (MCSEs) exceeded the `0.005` screen on `486` directional entries
(maximum `0.005867`), while its chain-based MCSE for the fixed grading's
aggregate loss was `0.000096` (`9.62e-05`, below the `0.001` target): aggregate
loss averages across `2,211` pairs and can be estimated much more precisely
than individual borderline pairs. Pairs where all retained draws fell on one
side (`0` or `1` frequencies) have zero sample variance across draws (so their
chain MCSE is unavailable rather than proving posterior certainty), and
agreement between pools A and B does not validate the model on external data.

## Substantive scope and data attribution {#use-the-result-and-retain-its-scope}

In this historical Alabama cohort, requiring one common grading across adult
income and incarceration leaves `43.5%` of county pairs unordered, agrees with
expected-rank contiguous cuts, and yields different expected error rates across
the two outcomes (`5.2%` versus `17.2%`). Choosing between one common grading
and separate outcome-specific gradings is a policy choice about what the report
must communicate.

Data attribution: Raj Chetty, John Friedman, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie R.
Jones, and Sonya R. Porter (2022), *Replication Data for: The Opportunity
Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility*, Harvard Dataverse V1.0,
[doi:10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1); source:
Opportunity Insights and the U.S. Census Bureau
([county CSV](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/county_outcomes_simple.csv)),
used under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Adaptations include filtering to Alabama, adding county identifiers and names,
scaling units and negating incarceration, fitting separate hierarchical models,
and extracting compact pairwise probabilities and 95% intervals; no endorsement
by the original authors or agencies is implied.
